newsitem.title: HONG KONG: All eyes on U.S. election as Asian markets edge up.
newsitem.headline: All eyes on U.S. election as Asian markets edge up.

text.p: Asian markets on Monday defied the conventional wisdom that drifting shares generally head lower, with most bourses posting small gains in quiet trade ahead of U.S. presidential election.

Jakarta was the day's star performer, with the composite index rising 7.65 points, or 1.34 percent, to 578.31. Brokers said overall trade was slow with the public offering by Bank Negara Indonesia, which opened today, the major focus.
Hong Kong's Hang Seng index managed to eke out a new closing high, aided by a jump in New World Development shares ahead of the release of the company's results this week.
The index closed 30.13 points higher at 12,559.40. Turnover was HK$6.34 billion, compared to HK$7.3 billion on Friday.

"The market has still done reasonably well given the situation in the U.S.," said Alan Hutcheson, director of research at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell. "At the end of the day it's New World that is really keeping it there."

Analysts said caution ahead of Tuesday's U.S. presidential election had kept some investors sidelined. They said investors were nervous that a Democratic sweep of the Congressional races would prompt weakness on Wall Street.

Singapore, Malaysia, New Zealand and Thailand were all quiet ahead of the U.S. poll. Singapore's STI index rose 7.61 points to 2,075.78, Kuala Lumpur's composite index put on 4.59 to 1,177.07, while Wellington's top 40 index closed off 7.9 points at 2,314.5. Bangkok's SET index closed up 0.45 point at 912.97.
In Australia, hopes of an interest rate cut hoisted shares higher although trade remained lacklustre as players awaited the result of the Reserve Bank's deliberations on Tuesday.
The All Ordinaries index rose 18.1 points to 2,357.5.

With the recent spate of economic data sparking speculation of when, rather than if, interest rates would be cut, those traders willing to play the game pushed the market solidly higher in the afternoon session.

"There is a possibility of the Reserve Bank will make their announcement tomorrow (Tuesday) about an interest rate cut, if any, and that has had a beneficial effect on the banks, all of which are up quite strongly," said broker Kevin Lourey of Melbourne brokerage Peake Lands Kirwan.
Taiwan shares also closed sharply higher, with confidence rising after the government announced it was freeing two major state funds to invest in stocks, brokers said.
The weighted index ended 59.67 points or 0.91 percent higher at 6,622.61, the market's highest close since October 14.

South Korean shares ended below the psychological support level of 750 on concerns about an oversupply of shares in November, brokers said. Seoul's composite stock index closed at a provisional 747.42, down 18.31 points, or 2.39 percent.
Philippine shares ended slightly higher after a slow opening, shored up by selected bargain-hunting. The main index closed up 12.14 points, or 0.41 percent, at 2,976.14 points.
In India, Bombay's BSE Sensex index shed 55.85 points to close at a provisional 3,092.72, hammered by the continuing foreign exchange scandal involving tobacco company ITC.
Tokyo was closed for a holiday on Monday, but trading will resume on Tuesday. Analysts said the Japanese market was likely to keep up its search for a floor in the week ahead.
The dollar weakened against the yen in Asian trade after earlier gains on reports of a possible military coup in Russia. At 1154 GMT the dollar was quoted at 113.16/26 yen and 1.5130/33 marks.

Hong Kong's gold market on Monday edged slightly above New York's previous close, buoyed by European buying and continued physical demand, dealers and traders said. Bullion ended at US$378.30/80 an ounce against New York's US$378.00/50 close on Friday.

SIMEX Brent futures edged up in late afternoon trade on slim volumes, helped by a perception that the market would correct higher. Brent December last traded at US$22.55 a barrel, up five cents from London's settlement on Friday.
